entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Siege of Orléans, which took place from October 1428 to May 1429, was a pivotal event in the Hundred Years' War between France and England. This 55-day siege was led by Joan of Arc and the French army, who successfully repelled the English forces led by Sir John Fastolf. The siege was a crucial turning point in the war, as it led to the eventual coronation of Charles VII of France and the expulsion of the English from the region.

The siege was a testament to the bravery and determination of the French people, who fought tirelessly to defend their city against the English invaders. The involvement of Joan of Arc, who led the charge against the English, added a layer of spiritual and symbolic significance to the event. Her leadership and conviction helped to galvanize the French army and secure a much-needed victory.

The legacy of the Siege of Orléans can be seen in the impact it had on the outcome of the Hundred Years' War. The French victory marked a significant shift in the balance of power between France and England, paving the way for the eventual French dominance in the region. The siege also cemented Joan of Arc's place in history as a heroine and a symbol of French resistance.

As Joan of Arc herself said, 'God willing, I shall go to Orléans. I shall ride at the head of the army, and I shall raise the siege.' Her words encapsulate the spirit of the siege, which was a defining moment in the history of France and a testament to the power of courage and conviction in the face of overwhelming odds.
